0.0.n: ボカージュ is borrowed from French and describes countryside divided into fields by hedges.

0.1.n: は marks ボカージュ as the topic of the sentence.

0.2.n: 私 combines with たち to refer to the speaker and her group.

0.3.n: This suffix makes 私 plural: 私たち refers to the speaker's group.

0.4.n: にとって marks whose perspective or experience the statement describes.

0.5.n: This noun modifies 裏庭 through の.

0.6.n: の connects 宮殿 to 裏庭, showing which building the yard belongs to.

0.7.n: This is the place the speaker compares the bocage to.

0.8.n: みたい makes a casual comparison, rather than saying the two things are identical.

0.9.n: な connects みたい to the following noun もの.

0.10.n: もの gives the comparison a general sense: something resembling a palace backyard.

0.11.n: だ is the plain statement form used after a noun.

0.12.n: Sentence-ending わ adds a feminine tone to this statement.

1.0.n: 干し芋 literally refers to dried sweet potato; here it serves as a nickname for the opposing group.

1.1.n: さん is a respectful suffix attached to the nickname 干し芋.

1.2.n: たち indicates the people associated with the nickname, not multiple sweet potatoes.

1.3.n: は introduces the opposing group as the topic.

1.4.n: This borrowed term refers here to resistance fighters, evoking their guerrilla tactics.

1.5.n: の connects レジスタンス to よう in the comparison pattern のような.

1.6.n: よう expresses resemblance; here it compares the fighting to that of resistance fighters.

1.7.n: な lets のよう describe the following noun 遊撃戦.

1.8.n: This noun refers to fighting through mobile, surprise attacks rather than direct confrontation.

1.9.n: を marks 遊撃戦 as what the opposing group fears.

1.10.n: 恐れている is 恐れる in the て-form plus いる, describing an ongoing state of fear.

1.11.n: から follows the reason for the prediction in the next clause.

1.13.n: 容易 combines with に to describe how readily they would act.

1.14.n: に turns 容易 into a description of how an action happens.

1.15.n: は highlights 容易に; with the negative ending, it suggests they will not act readily.

1.16.n: 手 is part of 手を出す, an expression for intervening or making an aggressive move.

1.17.n: を connects 手 to 出す within the expression 手を出す.

1.18.n: 出してこない combines 出す with negative くる, presenting the action as directed toward the speaker's side.

1.19.n: Sentence-ending の gives the statement an explanatory tone.

2.0.n: じっくり describes proceeding carefully and without rushing.

2.1.n: 行きましょう is the polite invitation form of 行く, suggesting a shared course of action.

3.0.n: 最も places the following quality at its highest degree.

3.1.n: This adjective directly describes 人 and emphasizes the ability to endure without giving up.

3.2.n: 人 is described by 最も辛抱強い and receives victory in this saying.

3.3.n: に marks the person toward whom victory comes.

3.4.n: This noun is presented as something that arrives at a person.

3.5.n: は makes 勝利 the topic, even though the recipient appears first.

3.6.n: やってくる emphasizes arrival; here victory is figuratively pictured as coming to someone.

3.7.n: の adds an explanatory tone to the saying before it is quoted.

3.9.n: って is a casual quotation marker, linking the preceding saying to 言ってた.

3.10.n: 誰 combines with か to refer to an unspecified person.

3.11.n: か changes the question word 誰 into 誰か, referring to an unspecified person.

3.12.n: が marks 誰か as the person who said the quoted words.

3.13.n: 言ってた is the casual shortening of 言っていた, recalling something someone said previously.

3.14.n: Sentence-ending わ adds a feminine tone to the speaker's recollection.

0.lit: The bocage, for us, is something like a palace's backyard.
0.tip: 私たちにとって sets the perspective: the comparison is true from the speaker's group's point of view.

1.lit: Dried Sweet Potato's group fears Resistance-like guerrilla warfare, so they will not easily put a hand out toward us.
1.tip: 手を出す literally mentions putting out a hand, but here means making an aggressive move.

2.tip: The polite ましょう ending invites others to do something together.

3.lit: To the most patient person, victory comes—that, someone was saying.
3.tip: って marks the preceding sentence as a quotation, even though it comes after a subtitle sentence break.
